617.title: Mud and spit (John 9:1–12)
617.hook: who sinned, this man or his parents? neither; he makes clay and says go wash
617.howItsDone: Christians often read this chapter in Lent, and many churches connect the washing in Siloam with baptism, which early Christians sometimes called illumination.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sentence carved in stone, and its quieter first half: if ye continue in my word. Your line was the truth shall make you free. Did you say your true thing? Day six hundred seventeen.

When something terrible happens, people reach for a reason. Somebody must have done something. A diagnosis, an accident, a child born with a disability, and the question comes, out loud or whispered: what did they do to deserve this? It's an old question. Jesus and his friends are walking along, and they pass a man who has been blind since birth. And the disciples, without even lowering their voices, turn him into a theology problem. "Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?" The man can hear them.

The disciples give Jesus two choices. Either the man sinned, somehow, or his parents did. Jesus refuses both. "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." Neither. The blindness isn't a punishment. Christians have wrestled with the second half of that verse. Does it mean God made him blind just to make a point? Some readers answer by moving the full stop: neither this man sinned nor his parents. Period. Then: so that the works of God may be shown, we must work while it is day. Read that way, Jesus doesn't explain the blindness. He moves straight from blame to work. Then he does something earthy. "He spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay." Mud and spit. Not a word from a distance this time, like with the official's son. Touch. Some early Christian writers saw an echo of Genesis, where God forms the first human from the dust of the ground. Then: "Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.)" The man has to walk there, still blind, mud on his face, through the streets of Jerusalem. "He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing." A handful of words for a whole new life. And the pool is real. Workers repairing a pipe in Jerusalem uncovered stone steps of a large pool from Jesus's time, which archaeologists identify as Siloam.
screen: `MUD AND SPIT, LIKE DUST IN EDEN.`
then, large: `NEITHER HATH THIS MAN SINNED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop blaming someone's pain. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is suffering. A friend, a stranger in the news, maybe yourself. Notice if somewhere in you there's a quiet explanation. They should have known. They brought it on themselves. I must deserve this. You don't have to argue with it. Just notice it, and set it down. Then ask the question Jesus moved to instead: what work could I do here? A call, a meal, a ride, a kind word. If you pray, you can hold that person before God without explanations. If you don't, just hold them with care. The bell holds the time.
Mud and spit. How Jesus healed a man born blind: clay on his eyes, and a walk to the pool called Sent.
Your line: neither sinned. Today, when you hear someone blame a person for their own pain, or catch yourself doing it, skip the reason and look for the work. Day six hundred seventeen.

618.title: Now I see (John 9:13–41)
618.hook: the healed man is questioned, thrown out, and found again by Jesus
618.howItsDone: Christians often share testimonies, simple accounts of what God has done in their lives, and the healed man's "one thing I know" is a common model; the hymn Amazing Grace echoes his words.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mud and spit, a walk to the pool called Sent, and a man who came back seeing. Your line was neither sinned. Did you skip the blame and find the work? Day six hundred eighteen.

A miracle ought to end in a party. A man blind from birth can see. His neighbors should be throwing a feast. Instead, chapter nine becomes a courtroom drama. The neighbors argue about whether it's even him. Some say yes. Others say no, he just looks like him. And the man keeps saying, over and over, I am he. Then he's brought to the religious leaders, and the questions start. How did this happen? Who did it? Was it the sabbath? The man who was blind is about to be questioned three times, and he gets braver each time.

The first time, he just tells the facts: he put clay on my eyes, I washed, and I see. The leaders are divided. Some say a man who heals on the sabbath can't be from God. Others say, how can a sinner do such signs? They ask the healed man what he thinks. He says: he's a prophet. Then they call his parents. And his parents, frightened, say only: yes, this is our son, and yes, he was born blind. How he sees, we don't know. Ask him. He's of age. John says they were afraid of being put out of the synagogue. Some readers think this detail also reflects John's own time, when followers of Jesus and other Jewish communities were painfully parting ways. So the man is called back a second time, and pressed: we know this man is a sinner. And he answers: "whether he be a sinner or no, I know not: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see." He doesn't win the theology argument. He doesn't try. He stands on the one thing he's sure of. Then he even gets cheeky: why do you want to hear it again? Will ye also be his disciples? And they throw him out. Here's the turn. "Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he had found him," he asks: do you believe in the Son of man? Who is he, Lord? You've seen him. He's talking with you. And the man says, "Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him." Thrown out by one door, he's found by the one who came looking.
screen: then, large: `WHEREAS I WAS BLIND, NOW I SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand by your one sure thing. Settle, and breathe. Think about the big questions you can't answer. About God, about suffering, about what happens next. Let them be there, unresolved. Now look for one thing you know from your own life. Something you've seen with your own eyes. A time you were helped. A change in you. A moment of beauty you can't explain away. Hold it simply, without arguing for it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, just let it be solid ground. The bell holds the time.
Now I see. The healed man's answer to his questioners: one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see.
Your line: now I see. Today, when someone asks how you are or what you believe, tell one thing you know firsthand, simply, without a speech. Day six hundred eighteen.

619.title: I am the gate (John 10:1–10)
619.hook: I came that they may have life, and have it abundantly
619.howItsDone: Christians often quote John 10:10 when describing the life they hope faith brings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man questioned three times, thrown out, and found again. Your line was now I see. What one thing did you say you know? Day six hundred nineteen.

A sheepfold on a hillside: a rough circle of stone walls, chest high, with one gap for an opening. At night the sheep are led inside, safe from wolves and thieves. Jesus is still talking to the same listeners as yesterday, the ones who threw the healed man out, and he tells them a picture-story about sheep, a gatekeeper, thieves who climb over the wall, and a shepherd who walks in through the door. John says plainly that they didn't understand it. So Jesus tries again, more directly.

First, the shepherd. The sheep hear his voice, and "he calleth his own sheep by name, and leadeth them out." Notice how personal that is. Not a herd. Names. Then the surprise: "I am the door: by me if any man enter in, he shall be saved, and shall go in and out, and find pasture." The King James says door. Some modern Bibles say gate. Either way, it's the opening in the wall. John has given us I am sayings before: bread, light. Now, the way in. People often tell how a shepherd in that region, at night, might lie down across the gap in the wall and sleep there, so that nothing could get in or out without stepping over him. Whether or not every shepherd did that, it's a good picture of what Jesus is saying. Look at the words: go in and out. A gate isn't only for locking in. It's for safety at night and freedom in the morning. In, to rest. Out, to pasture. Then the verse behind today's line: "The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly." The Greek word behind abundantly means more than enough, overflowing, beyond what's needed. Not just surviving. Not just getting by. Life with something left over. Christians often hold this line as a picture of what faith is meant to be: not a smaller life fenced in by rules, but a bigger one, with a safe place to come home to.

Here's the practice: choose one abundant thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of your day as it's going to go. How much of it is just getting by? Errands, emails, getting through. That's real, and it's fine. Now picture one small thing you could add that is more than necessary. A longer walk. A real conversation. Cooking something properly. Ten minutes outside. Music you love, played loud. Choose one. If you pray, you can give thanks for the life you have, and ask for it in full. If you don't, just savor the thought of the thing you chose. The bell holds the time.
I am the gate. One of Jesus's I am sayings in John: the way into the fold, for safety at night and pasture by day.
Your line: life to the full. Today, do the one abundant thing you chose, and do it without hurrying. Day six hundred nineteen.

620.title: The good shepherd (John 10:11–18)
620.hook: he knows his sheep and lays down his life
620.howItsDone: Many churches keep a Good Shepherd Sunday in the Easter season, and the image of Christ carrying a sheep remains common in stained glass, children's Bibles and church art.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a gap in a stone wall, and Jesus saying: I am the door. Your line was life to the full. What abundant thing did you choose? Day six hundred twenty.

Go down into the catacombs under Rome, the underground burial passages of the early Christians, and look at the painted walls. Long before the cross became the most common Christian image, one picture shows up again and again: a young man with a sheep across his shoulders, holding its legs in front of his chest. Some of these paintings go back to the two hundreds, the third century. When the first Christians wanted to picture Jesus near the graves of the people they loved, this is the picture many of them chose. It comes from today's words.

"I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep." This is the fourth I am saying in John, right on the heels of the door. The word for good is kalos, which means good and also beautiful, noble, the real thing. Not just a shepherd who does the job. The shepherd as he ought to be. Jesus sets him beside someone else: the hired hand. The hireling, as the King James calls him, sees a wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and runs. Not because he's evil. Because they're not his sheep. He's paid by the day. The good shepherd stays, because they're his own. And then a line of real tenderness: "I am the good shepherd, and know my sheep, and am known of mine." Knowing goes both ways. He knows them, and they know him. Shepherding pictures run deep in the scriptures Jesus grew up with. King David was a shepherd. Psalm twenty-three begins, the Lord is my shepherd. In Ezekiel, God condemns shepherds who feed themselves instead of the flock, and promises to search for the lost sheep himself. Jesus steps into that old picture. He adds: "And other sheep I have, which are not of this fold." Christians have long read that as a sign the flock would grow wider than anyone listening expected. And the most striking part: he says no one takes his life from him. "I lay it down of myself." The good shepherd isn't caught off guard. He chooses to give his life for the sheep, freely.
screen: then, large: `I LAY IT DOWN OF MYSELF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: know someone's name and use it. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people you see often but don't really know. The person at the coffee shop. A neighbor. The security guard. Someone at work you nod to. Do you know their names? Pick one person whose name you know, or would like to learn. Picture saying it to them, warmly, today. Then remember a time someone used your name when you didn't expect them to know it, and how that felt. If you pray, you can give thanks that you're known by name. If you don't, just hold the feeling of being known. The bell holds the time.
The good shepherd. The fourth of Jesus's I am sayings in John: the shepherd who knows his sheep, and lays down his life for them.
Your line: I know my own. Today, learn one name you didn't know, or use one you did, and look the person in the eye when you say it. Day six hundred twenty.

621.title: At the feast of Dedication (John 10:22–42)
621.hook: in winter, at Hanukkah in Solomon's porch, they ask him plainly
621.howItsDone: Jews keep Hanukkah for eight nights each winter, lighting one more light each night; Christians read this passage as Jesus's plain claim of unity with the Father and a promise that his own are held safe.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a painting in the catacombs, and the good shepherd who knows his sheep. Your line was I know my own. Whose name did you learn or use? Day six hundred twenty-one.

"And it was at Jerusalem the feast of the dedication, and it was winter." Two little facts, and they set a whole scene. The feast of the dedication is Hanukkah. The feast's own story is told in First Maccabees, a book that Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include. And it's winter, cold enough that Jesus is walking under cover, in the colonnade called Solomon's porch. A crowd gathers around him there, close, maybe blocking his way. And they ask the question that has followed him for chapters.

First, the feast. Long before Jesus, a Greek king named Antiochus the Fourth set up pagan worship in the temple in Jerusalem and tried to stamp out Jewish practice. A family called the Maccabees led a revolt. When they took back the temple, they cleansed it and dedicated it again, with an eight-day celebration. The book of First Maccabees describes it. Hanukkah means dedication. The famous story of a small jar of oil burning for eight days is told later, in the Talmud. Jews keep Hanukkah to this day, lighting lights in winter. So here is Jesus, at the feast that remembers the temple made holy again. And the crowd says: "How long dost thou make us to doubt? If thou be the Christ, tell us plainly." His answer: I've told you, and the works I do tell you. My sheep hear my voice. Then a promise: "And I give unto them eternal life; and they shall never perish, neither shall any man pluck them out of my hand." Pluck is the King James word. Some modern Bibles say snatch, like a wolf grabbing a lamb. And then he goes further: no one can pluck them out of my Father's hand. "I and my Father are one." The crowd hears it as blasphemy and picks up stones again. He escapes across the Jordan, to the place where John baptized at the very start. And there, John says, many believed. The story circles back to where it began.
screen: then, large: `I AND MY FATHER ARE ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: light a light for the winter. If there's a candle or lamp nearby, light it or switch it on. If not, picture one. Settle, and breathe. Watch the light for a moment. Think of someone going through a winter right now: grief, illness, loneliness, fear. Picture them held safe, in hands that won't let go. Then think of your own winter, if you're in one. If you pray, you can hold that person, and yourself, in the promise that no one can snatch them away. If you don't, simply keep the light company. The bell holds the time.
Hanukkah. The Jewish feast of the dedication, remembering the temple cleansed and dedicated again. Jesus walked in the temple at Hanukkah, in winter.
Your line: no one can snatch them. Today, send one message to the person in a winter you thought of, so they know they're held. Day six hundred twenty-one.

622.title: I am the resurrection (John 11:1–27)
622.hook: Martha meets him on the road and makes her confession
622.howItsDone: Jesus's words to Martha are often read at Christian funerals; in the Book of Common Prayer burial service, they are the first words said as the body is brought to the church.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hanukkah in winter, under Solomon's porch, and a promise about hands that won't let go. Your line was no one can snatch them. Who did you send a message to? Day six hundred twenty-two.

A message arrives across the Jordan from two sisters in Bethany, a village just outside Jerusalem. It's short, and it doesn't ask for anything directly: "Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." Their brother Lazarus. The one you love. John adds, so we can't miss it: "Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus." And then the strangest sentence. Right after telling us he loved them, John says that when Jesus heard Lazarus was sick, he stayed where he was two more days. John doesn't explain the wait. Not yet.

When Jesus finally says, let's go back to Judea, the disciples are alarmed. They tried to stone you there. Thomas, the one later remembered for doubting, says something brave and bleak: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." By the time they reach Bethany, Lazarus has been in the tomb four days. Friends have come from Jerusalem to comfort the sisters. And Martha, hearing Jesus is near, doesn't wait at home. She goes out to meet him on the road. Her first words are honest, almost an accusation: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Then, in the same breath, she says she knows God will give him whatever he asks. Jesus says: your brother will rise again. Martha answers with a hope she already holds, a resurrection of the dead at the end of time: "I know that he shall rise again in the resurrection at the last day." Someday. Far off. And Jesus brings it into the present tense: "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." Not, there will be a resurrection. I am. Then he asks her directly: believest thou this? And Martha makes her confession: "Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world." In Matthew's Gospel, it's Peter who says something like this. In John, it's Martha, standing on a road, grieving, with her brother four days in the tomb.
screen: then, large: `I AM THE RESURRECTION, AND THE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say what you believe out loud. Settle, and breathe. Martha said two things at once: if you had been here, and I believe. Grief and faith in the same breath. Think about what you actually believe today, whatever it is. It might be about God. It might be simpler: that love matters, that people can change, that the person you lost still matters. Find one sentence that's true for you. Then, quietly, say it out loud. Hear your own voice say it. If you pray, you can say it to God, the way Martha did. If you don't, say it to the room. The bell holds the time.
I am the resurrection. One of Jesus's I am sayings in John, spoken to Martha on the road, with her brother four days in the tomb.
Your line: I am the resurrection. Today, if grief or disappointment comes up, let it sit beside what you believe, the way Martha held both on the road. Day six hundred twenty-two.

623.title: Jesus wept (John 11:28–44)
623.hook: he weeps with Mary, then calls Lazarus out and says: unbind him
623.howItsDone: Christians often turn to "Jesus wept" in times of grief, as a sign that mourning is not a failure of faith; the raising of Lazarus is read in some churches in Lent, and the Orthodox Church keeps Lazarus Saturday before Palm Sunday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Martha met Jesus on the road and made her confession. Your line was I am the resurrection. Did you let grief and faith sit side by side? Day six hundred twenty-three.

Martha goes home and whispers to her sister: the Master is here, and he's asking for you. Mary gets up quickly and goes out. The mourners in the house follow her, thinking she's going to the tomb to weep there. She finds Jesus, falls at his feet, and says exactly the same words her sister said: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Same sentence, different sister. But this time Jesus doesn't answer with a teaching. No I am. No question. He looks at her, crying, and at the people crying with her.

John says "he groaned in the spirit, and was troubled." The Greek word for groaned is strong, almost angry, a deep shudder. He asks where they've laid him. Come and see, they say, the same words Jesus used to his first disciples, now used to lead him to a grave. And then: "Jesus wept." Two words in the King James Bible, and a whole verse. He knows what he's about to do. He's just told Martha, I am the resurrection. And he weeps anyway. John lets grief and faith stand side by side. The people watching say: "Behold how he loved him!" At the tomb, a cave with a stone across it, he says, take away the stone. And Martha, practical to the end, objects: "Lord, by this time he stinketh: for he hath been dead four days." Jesus prays aloud, then cries with a loud voice: "Lazarus, come forth." And the dead man comes out, still wrapped hand and foot in grave clothes, his face bound with a cloth. Then the last command, the one that gives us today's line: "Loose him, and let him go." Notice who does the unbinding. Not Jesus. The people standing around. Jesus calls Lazarus to life; the community unwraps him. This week we've walked a long way: mud and spit, now I see, the door, the good shepherd, Hanukkah in winter, Martha on the road, and now tears at a tomb, and a man walking out of it.
screen: then, large: `LOOSE HIM, AND LET HIM GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help unbind someone. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you know who has come through something hard, an illness, a loss, an addiction, a bad season, but is still wrapped in it. Still carrying the old cloths. Picture them. What's still binding them? Loneliness, shame, a practical problem, a debt, other people's memories of who they were? Ask what small part of that you could help loosen. A ride, a meal, an invitation, forgetting the old story. If you pray, you can hold them before God. If you don't, just hold them in mind kindly. The bell holds the time.
Jesus wept. Two words in the King James Bible: Jesus weeping with Mary at his friend's grave, moments before calling him out.
Your line: loose him, let him go. Today, do one small thing to help unwrap the person you thought of. Day six hundred twenty-three, and another week on the path.

he told the people: "loose him, and let him go."

fork.setup: you're standing at the tomb. Jesus says: take away the stone. you're Martha. what do you say?
fork.reveal: practical Martha warns him: four days dead. Jesus answers that she'll see the glory of God, and the stone is moved.

original.note: Greek: he shed tears. A quieter word than the loud wailing of the mourners around him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a two-word verse, good for a trivia question.
what it means: Jesus, about to raise his friend, weeps anyway, and then calls the community to unbind him.
what a scholar hears: edakrusen, he shed tears, differs from the word John uses for the mourners' weeping.
